\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{शंखः} (śaṅkhaḥ)}{शंखः (śaṅkhaḥ)}]{\sk{शंखः} (śaṅkhaḥ) — a conch}

\label{lesson:SA-C161-sankhah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for eating, then the Sanskrit for a small pitcher.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शंखः}}
\textbf{\sk{शंखः}} — \emph{śaṅkhaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a conch\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{śaṅkha} \textquotedblleft{}a conch-shell\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Atharvaveda, and is inherited from Indo-European: MW sets it beside Greek \emph{konchē} and Latin \emph{concha} \textquotedblleft{}shell\textquotedblright{}, and EtymDB agrees. It lives on as Hindi \emph{saṅkh} \textquotedblleft{}conch\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 12263).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वेणुः} (veṇuḥ)}{वेणुः (veṇuḥ)}]{\sk{वेणुः} (veṇuḥ) — a flute}

\label{lesson:SA-C161-venuh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a small pitcher, then the Sanskrit for a conch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वेणुः}}
\textbf{\sk{वेणुः}} — \emph{veṇuḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a flute\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{veṇu} first meant \textquotedblleft{}a bamboo, a reed\textquotedblright{} in the Rigveda and later \textquotedblleft{}a flute\textquotedblright{} (MW). MW thinks it probably comes from the root √ve \textquotedblleft{}weave\textquotedblright{}, but CDIAL 12096 finds its connections unclear, so its origin is uncertain.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{मृदंगः} (mṛdaṅgaḥ)}{मृदंगः (mṛdaṅgaḥ)}]{\sk{मृदंगः} (mṛdaṅgaḥ) — a mridanga drum}

\label{lesson:SA-C161-mrdangah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a conch, then the Sanskrit for a flute.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मृदंगः}}
\textbf{\sk{मृदंगः}} — \emph{mṛdaṅgaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a mridanga drum\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
MW explains \emph{mṛdaṅga} \textquotedblleft{}a drum\textquotedblright{} as probably \emph{mṛdam} + \emph{-ga}, \textquotedblleft{}going about while being beaten\textquotedblright{}, from the root √mṛd \textquotedblleft{}press, beat\textquotedblright{}. CDIAL 10289 compares \emph{mardala}, another drum, so the formation is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नूपुरम्} (nūpuram)}{नूपुरम् (nūpuram)}]{\sk{नूपुरम्} (nūpuram) — an anklet}

\label{lesson:SA-C161-nupuram}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a flute, then the Sanskrit for a mridanga drum.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नूपुरम्}}
\textbf{\sk{नूपुरम्}} — \emph{nūpuram} — \textquotedblleft{}an anklet\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nūpura} \textquotedblleft{}an anklet\textquotedblright{} has an uncertain origin: CDIAL 7577 reports both a Middle Indic form reshaped after \emph{keyūra} \textquotedblleft{}armlet\textquotedblright{} and Kuiper's non-Aryan account, comparing Santali \emph{lipur}. It lives on as Hindi and Punjabi \emph{neur} \textquotedblleft{}anklet\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7577).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कुण्डलम्} (kuṇḍalam)}{कुण्डलम् (kuṇḍalam)}]{\sk{कुण्डलम्} (kuṇḍalam) — an earring}

\label{lesson:SA-C161-kundalam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a mridanga drum, then the Sanskrit for an anklet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कुण्डलम्}}
\textbf{\sk{कुण्डलम्}} — \emph{kuṇḍalam} — \textquotedblleft{}an earring\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kuṇḍala} \textquotedblleft{}a ring, an earring\textquotedblright{} is taken to be borrowed from Dravidian, after Burrow (CDIAL 3268; EWA). It lives on as Punjabi \emph{kuṇḍal} \textquotedblleft{}coil, earring\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3268).
\end{cousinweb}
